description: Judge calibration tests. Protocol: for each problem, generate one correct reasoning chain and one deliberately flawed chain, score both with the judge, then measure (a) Spearman r between judge score and correct/flawed label, and (b) separation rate — the fraction of problems where correct scored above flawed.
provenance: exact — transcribed from Colab run logs

pass_thresholds.note: Thresholds were set a priori. StrategyQA was accepted at r=0.531 / 85% after analysis showed the shortfall is a judge world-knowledge limitation rather than a design flaw.

production.status: PASS — used for all GSM8K training
production.note: Point estimate exceeds GPT-4.1-mini (0.734 vs 0.600), but at n=20 the 95% CI is [0.43, 0.89] against GPT-4.1-mini's [0.45, 0.72] at n=93 — the intervals overlap almost entirely and the comparison is NOT statistically supported. Separation rates overlap likewise (19/20 -> [0.76, 0.99]; 84/93 -> [0.83, 0.95]). The defensible claim is that the open-weight 7B judge is competitive with GPT-4.1-mini and removes the closed-weight API dependency, not that it beats it. n~80 would be needed for the lower bound to clear 0.600.

window_size_ablation.conclusion: W>=3 scored higher (0.690 vs 0.600) and the window distribution was set to {2:0.1, 3:0.5, 5:0.4} on that basis. Both figures come from n=20 calibration sets, where a 0.09 difference in Spearman r is well inside noise. Treat this as a preliminary read that informed a design choice, not as an ablation.

qwen_7b.status: PASS — used for all StrategyQA training
qwen_7b.caveat: r=0.531 at n=20 has a 95% CI of [0.12, 0.79]. The lower bound is close to zero, so this judge's calibration cannot be distinguished from weak. It produced the reward signal behind the cross-task transfer result, which makes widening n here the highest-value validation work available.

qwen_32b.finding: Larger judge is not automatically better. 32B underperformed 7B on both r and separation. Hypothesis: 32B generates more nuanced correct-and-flawed chains that are harder to separate, and produces less decisive scores. Note the CIs on the 7B and 32B StrategyQA runs overlap substantially at n=20; 'larger is not better' is a suggestive observation here, not a result.

math.summary: All three open-weight judges failed. MATH training was abandoned.

qwen_math_7b.failure_mode: Model ignores the SCORE output format entirely and emits its own full solution instead ('To evaluate the quality of the step-by-step reasoning, let's analyze each step carefully...'). A constraining system prompt had no effect. Its instruction tuning for math-solving overrides grader-role instructions. Every window fell back to the neutral 0.5 default, producing identical scores for correct and flawed chains.

qwen_32b.note: Format compliance was perfect (every window returned a valid SCORE). The failure is capability, not formatting.

math.root_cause: Detecting an injected algebraic error requires independently solving the problem. No open-weight model at 7B-32B scale does this reliably for competition math. Note the pattern across all three judges: the relevance dimension separates well (4-5/6) while the algebraic dimension does not (0-2/7). Relevance is checkable without solving; algebraic validity is not. This is a capability ceiling, not a prompt-engineering problem.

uncertainty_note: Confidence intervals added post hoc (95%). Spearman r: Fisher z-transform. Separation rate: Wilson score interval. Most of these calibration runs used n=20, which yields intervals wide enough that several pairwise comparisons in this file are not statistically separable. See the per-entry caveats. Widening n is the single cheapest improvement available to this project — judge calibration is inference only, requiring no training.
